data.copy:
After my pedicure, my nail tech asked: 'Can I ask why you do it that way?' I had no idea what she meant. I'm 69 years old.

I've been getting monthly pedicures at the same salon for twelve years.

And I've been apologizing for my legs every single time.

Last Wednesday at 2:15 PM, sitting in the pedicure chair with my feet in warm water, I did it 
again.

"Sorry about the stubble," I said to Tina, my nail tech. "I shaved yesterday but you can 
probably already see it coming back."

I always say this. Every month. For twelve years.

Tina has seen my legs more than anyone except me. The razor burn on my ankles. The 
nicks that take forever to heal. The stubble that's visible by day two no matter how carefully I 
shave.

She's always been polite. Never commented. Just smiled and said "You're fine" and started 
the pedicure.

But this time, she put down the foot file and looked at me.

"Can I tell you something?"

"Sure."

"You're my only client who still shaves their legs."

I stared at her. "What?"

"Out of everyone I see. And I see maybe forty women a week. You're the only one who 
shaves."

I felt my face get hot. "That can't be right."

"It is. You're the only one who apologizes for stubble. The only one with razor burn. The only 
one with nicks healing on their ankles. Everyone else uses cream."

I sat there with my feet in the water feeling like the floor had dropped out.

"Everyone?"

"Every other woman I see. Young, old, doesn't matter. They all use depilatory cream. I 
thought you knew. I've been doing nails for fifteen years. You're the only person who still 
shaves."

Out of hundreds of women.

Thousands of legs she'd seen over the years.

And I was the only one.

"But... why didn't you say something?"
"I thought maybe you had a reason. Or maybe you preferred it. But every month you 
apologize. You seem embarrassed. And I finally realized you probably just don't know there's 
another way."

I was two seconds away from sending these back. Three days in and I'm thinking, what is this junk? £69 down the drain. Or so I thought.

But I'm getting ahead of myself. Let me start from the beginning.

I'm 71. Retired builder. Built half the houses on the new development off the A46. Forty-three years, rain or shine.

The hearing went gradually. You don't notice at first. People mumble. The TV speakers aren't what they used to be. Restaurants are too loud.

Margaret noticed before I did. Course she did.

'Jim, you've got the TV on thirty-eight.'

'It's fine.'

'The neighbours can hear Antiques Roadshow through the wall.'

But it wasn't fine. I knew it wasn't fine.

Family dinners were the worst. Twelve of us round the table. Everyone talking. Me, smiling and nodding. Catching maybe one word in five. My grandson Oliver telling some story about school. Me, laughing when everyone else laughed.

'Grandad's gone quiet,' my daughter said at our last family dinner.

I hadn't gone quiet. I'd gone deaf.

The NHS waiting list was sixteen months. Boots wanted £3,995. Specsavers, £1,995.

Did what every desperate old man does. Amazon. £59 hearing aids.

SCREEEEEECH. Feedback. Whistling. Everything loud except voices. Sent them back within a week.

For a year and a half, I did nothing. Stopped going to quiz night. Stopped answering the phone. Margaret started ordering for me in restaurants.

data.caption: dermiqua.com
data.copy:
I saw a statistic that made me sick. Women with actinic keratosis are 40 percent more likely to develop squamous cell carcinoma within five years if the underlying field damage goes untreated than women whose field is properly addressed.

Not a little more likely. Not the same. Forty percent.

I didn't believe it when I read it. I'd had rough patches on my arms and hands for almost 15 years and not one doctor had ever mentioned the field.

But here's the truth. Your dermatologist treats the spot she can see. The damaged keratinocytes spreading invisibly across the surrounding skin? Nobody is paid to look there.

That's why most of us never heard this.

That's why my mother never heard it either.

My mother was part of that statistic. Fourteen years of freeze sessions. Squamous cell carcinoma found on her forearm at 71.

I'm 63. Last month my dermatologist told me to come back every three months for another freeze and start monitoring more patches. I left the office and sat in my car for twenty minutes.

And what I found instead... in a small coastal Georgia farmers market on a Tuesday morning... took me from rough sandpaper patches covering both forearms and dreading every dermatologist visit... to smooth, even skin and wearing short sleeves to my granddaughter's recital. No more freeze sessions. No more "we'll keep watching."

But to understand why I was desperate enough to drive four hours to a farmers market at 6 AM, you have to know what I watched those freeze sessions do to my mother. And what I didn't know they were quietly not doing for me either.

For 14 YEARS... over a decade... my mother was trapped in the freeze-and-return cycle.

Started with liquid nitrogen. Her dermatologist called it "the gold standard." Said she'd need to come in every few months, but that was fine because it would keep the patches clear.

The patches did clear. For about six weeks.

Everything else got worse.

Miracle-Ear: $4,500. Costco: $1,500. Amazon: $50. Modern Hearing: $249. I spent three weeks finding out why those numbers are so different. The answer should be on the front page of every newspaper in America.

I built a pricing spreadsheet for every hearing aid option available in America.

I'm going to share it with you because I think every senior in this country deserves to see these numbers side by side.

I'm Jim. 73. Retired civil engineer from Ohio. Forty years building infrastructure. Cost analysis is not a new skill for me. I know what components cost. I know what fabrication costs. I know what markup looks like and I know how to follow a supply chain from a factory to a consumer price tag.

I did not apply that knowledge to hearing aids until my audiologist quoted me $4,800.

That afternoon I sat at my kitchen table and started building the spreadsheet.

Three weeks later I had something worth sharing.

**The price landscape — what every major option actually costs**

Let me put the numbers on the table before I explain what's behind them.

Miracle-Ear: $3,000 — $6,000 per pair
HearingLife: $2,800 — $5,600 per pair
Starkey (private clinic): $3,200 — $6,400 per pair
Best Buy (licensed audiologist): $1,600 — $2,400 per pair
Costco Hearing Center: $1,400 — $2,000 per pair
MDHearing Aid (OTC): $400 — $800 per pair
Eargo (OTC direct): $1,200 — $2,500 per pair
Amazon basic amplifiers: $30 — $200
Modern Hearing (direct): $249

Same general category of product. Price range from $30 to $6,400.

data.caption: Get Grounded While You Sleep
data.copy:
I found a piece of dried blueberry on my kitchen floor on a Sunday morning and I sat down on the linoleum and cried for 20 minutes.

That's where this story starts. Not in a doctor's office. Not at a hospital. On the floor of my kitchen in Springfield, Missouri, in my robe, at 7:14 in the morning, holding a piece of dried fruit that had rolled under the cabinet two days earlier and missed the broom.

My name is Cynthia. I'm 62 years old. I live in a yellow ranch house on Linwood Avenue that my husband Don and I bought in 1991 when our oldest was still in a stroller. Don passed in 2019. The house is too big for one person and I know it, but I'm not going anywhere because my granddaughter Wren lives 11 minutes away in a duplex with her mom (my daughter Rachel) and Wren has been coming over for Saturday morning blueberry pancakes since she was 4 years old.

She's 7 now.

That tradition is the one thing I have not let slip in three years of widowhood.

I make the batter from scratch. I use the cast iron my mother gave me when I got married. I cut the pancakes into shapes with cookie cutters because Wren still wants stars and hearts even though she'll tell you she's "too old" for that. I let her stand on a step stool and crack the eggs and she gets shell in the bowl every time and I pretend not to notice. We eat at the round oak table by the window. Two stacks. Maple syrup that I warm in a little pitcher because Don used to do it that way and I don't know how to do it any other way now.

That's what Saturdays are.

Or were.

Because something has been happening on those Saturdays for the last 14 months that I haven't told anybody.

Not Rachel.

Not my sister Donna.

Not my friend Carol from the church group.

Not even my doctor, who I saw in February and let me believe whatever I wanted to believe about how I was doing.

Here it is. The thing I haven't said out loud.

niches.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: CG, AM, GG, JY, GS, HT, BY, BG, SK, WC, MC, SP, KS, TS, HE, PS, DP, HI, FT, OG, OP, TR, AC, AA, BM, FK, SH, SW, EL, FW, WT, EW, FR, GM, PH, EC, WE, SC, BE, MU, PA, CB, CF, CP, DC, CT, HH, SG, YG, CC, PZ, LS, GP, WN, SF, OR, MG, PB. See allowed_niches in response for code→label map. Fashion/clothing = CG.

website.description: Detected store/checkout technology on the landing page (dashboard Website filter).
website.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: SH, TP, BU, LS, CC, SL, TA, GG, FU, CS, LP, FO, SI, GP, XS, YC, HY, DI, MS, SB, PP, WC, TT, TW, PI, GO, SC, FB, MG, WP, SQ, PS, GM, KV, CO, HJ, WX, AR, BC, MC. SH=Shopify, WC=WooCommerce, CS=Clickfunnels. See allowed_technologies in response.

languages.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

excludeLanguages.allowed_values: Comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

apps.description: Shopify apps detected on the store.
apps.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated app names/ids from dashboard Apps filter. See allowed_apps in response.

excludeApps.description: Exclude stores using these Shopify apps.
excludeApps.allowed_values: Comma-separated app names/ids. See allowed_apps in response.

themes.description: Shopify theme name on the store (exact match).
themes.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated exact theme names from dashboard Themes filter (discover via GET /api/themes).

scaling.allowed_values: rising, stable, declining, nodownscaling, upscaling, downscaling.

mediafilter.allowed_values: videos, images, carousel, dco. Omit/All = all formats.

pagetypefilter.allowed_values: products, collections, funnels, nofunnels. Empty/All = all types.

adscorefilter.description: WinningHunter ad score tier (Established / Has Potential / Unestablished).
adscorefilter.allowed_values: winning (Established), scaling (Has Potential), testing (Unestablished). Requires matching account tier.

lowimpressions.description: Hide ads with very low impressions.
lowimpressions.allowed_values: hide (exclude low-impression rows). Omit = show all.

rankgrowthfilter.description: Within-brand ad rank momentum vs historic rank_history.
rankgrowthfilter.allowed_values: Comma-separated subset of: rising, stable, declining.

minadrank.description: Minimum within-brand ad rank (lower rank number = stronger ad for that brand, e.g. #1).

min.description: Minimum duplicate/active-seen ad count on the page.

minactiveads.description: Minimum active Meta ads on the advertiser Facebook page (total_active_ads_on_page).
minactiveads.notes: find_winning_products auto-applies minactiveads=50 for US when not set (see forced block).

minactiveadsgrowth.description: Minimum page active-ads percent growth over activeadsgrowthperiod.
minactiveadsgrowth.allowed_values: Human percent (25 = 25%); negatives allowed for decline.

activeadsgrowthperiod.description: Lookback window for active-ads growth filter.
activeadsgrowthperiod.allowed_values: 1w, 1m, 3m. Default 1m when min/max growth set. 1w=1 week, 1m=1 month, 3m=3 months.
activeadsgrowthperiod.notes: 14d/2m exist on the dashboard but are omitted from MCP — sparse wlads baselines return empty result sets.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.
